source_text: Ecce enim nos, sicut primo libro fecimus, ita nunc presse cogimus, ut ostendas quemadmodum liberum arbitrium non negaris. Insidat autem hoc lectori nostro te videlicet confessum esse liberum arbitrium et Deum nascentium conditorem catholicis praedicare, quae duo numquam nisi Manichaeus negavit; sed cum haec communiter ambo dederimus nec tibi autem nec dogmati tuo libertas constet arbitrii, conficitur omnino te et dogma tuum de fide catholica nihil tenere. Interrogo ergo, quae vis sit quaeve definitio liberi arbitrii. Certe in eius potestate naturalium nulla conversio est. Nemo enim sensuum in se umquam mutavit officia, verbi gratia ut voces naribus aut auribus susciperet odores, nemo sexus sui convertit proprietatem, nemo in formam transire animantis alterius, nemo per liberum arbitrium pilos corporis sui innatis potuit mutare velleribus, nemo sibi pro ingenio aut qualitatem aut quantitatem corporis vindicavit. His exemplis licet omnia, quae ad hanc condicionem respiciunt, pervagari. Transeamus igitur a naturalibus ad externorum discussionem. Cui agrorum fecunditas, cui prosperitas navigationum, cui nobilitas et opes, cui constantia ipsius nobilitatis in iure constitit voluntatis, ut vel ad horum vel ad similium sibi conquisitionem voluntate se libera a Deo effectum esse fateretur? Naturalia ergo inconcussis ordinibus, externa vero casibus semper feruntur incertis. In quibus igitur liberum consistit arbitrium, propter quod homines bestiis antecellunt, propter quod ad Dei imaginem facti sunt et quo solo divini examinis iustitia continetur? In quo est hoc, inquam, arbitrium liberum, quod ut Manichaeos negare certum est, ita catholicos asserere etiam tu fateris? Sine dubio in eo, ut possibile sit homini voluntatem suam sine aliquo inevitabili naturalium coactu vel immittere in crimen vel a crimine cohibere.
pass_a_gloss: For behold we, as we did in the first book, so now closely compel, that you show how you have not denied free choice. But let this sit with our reader that you have confessed that catholics preach free choice and God the founder of those being born, which two never anyone except a Manichaean has denied; but when we have both given these commonly, yet neither to you nor to your dogma does the liberty of choice stand, it is altogether accomplished that you and your dogma hold nothing of the catholic faith. I ask therefore what is the force or what the definition of free choice. Certainly in its power there is no conversion of naturals. For no one has ever changed in himself the offices of the senses, for example that he receive voices by the nostrils or odors by the ears; no one has converted the property of his sex; no one into the form of another living being; no one through free choice could change the hairs of his body with inborn fleeces; no one has vindicated to himself for talent either the quality or the quantity of the body. By these examples it is permitted to wander through all things which look to this condition. Let us therefore pass from naturals to the discussion of externals. For whom has the fecundity of fields, for whom the prosperity of navigations, for whom nobility and riches, for whom the constancy of nobility itself stood in the right of will, that he would confess himself made by God with a free will either for the acquisition of these or of similar things? Naturals therefore are borne by unshaken orders, but externals always by uncertain chances. In what therefore does free choice consist, on account of which humans excel beasts, on account of which they have been made to the image of God and by which alone the justice of the divine examination is contained? In what is this, I say, free choice, which as it is certain the Manichaeans deny, so you also confess catholics assert? Without doubt in this, that it be possible for a human without any inevitable compulsion of naturals either to send his will into crime or to hold it from crime.

LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself

pass_b_english: Look: just as we did in the first book, we now press you closely to show how you have not denied free will. Let our reader remember that you have admitted catholics proclaim free will and God as the creator of newborn children—two things no one but a Manichaean ever denied. Yet although we both granted these in common, neither you nor your doctrine leaves freedom of choice intact. It follows completely that you and your doctrine retain nothing of the catholic faith.

I ask, then: what is the power of free will, and what is its definition? Certainly it has no power to change natural conditions. No one ever changed the functions of the senses within himself—for example, receiving sounds through the nose or smells through the ears. No one changed the characteristic of his sex; no one could pass into the form of another animal or, through free will, replace his body hair with a naturally grown fleece. No one could claim a body of whatever quality or size he wished. We may extend these examples to everything falling under this condition.

Let us move, then, from natural things to external circumstances. Whose will controls fruitful fields, successful voyages, noble birth and riches, or the continued standing of that nobility, so that he could say God made him with free will to acquire these or similar things for himself? Natural conditions follow fixed orders; external circumstances are always carried along by uncertain chances.

Where, then, does free will reside—the thing by which humans surpass beasts, by which they were made in God’s image (Genesis 1:26–27), and on which alone the justice of divine judgment rests? Where, I ask, is this free will, which the Manichaeans certainly deny and which you yourself admit catholics affirm? Undoubtedly in a person’s ability, without any unavoidable compulsion from natural conditions, either to direct his will into wrongdoing or to hold it back from wrongdoing.

choices.why: Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.
Julian's standing charge: natural evil is Manichaean. Keep the sect-name, not 'dualists'.
